title: Fashion Style Editing with Generative Human Prior
authors: Chaerin Kong, Seungyong Lee, Soohyeok Im, Wonsuk Yang
text:
Recent years have witnessed unprecedented progress in generative models [1,2,3,4,5], with the language guidance (i.e., text-to-image) being the cornerstone for their enhanced controllability and generalizability [6,7,8,9,10,11,12]. Image editing task [13,14,15] also started to draw great attention from the public thanks to the intuitive editing interface text-to-image frameworks provide [16,17,18]. One of the most popular ways to incorporate text condition to the image editing pipeline is to use a pretrained vision-language foundation model [19,20,21,22,23,24] as in StyleCLIP [17], CLIPstyler [13] or diffusionCLIP [25], where a joint embedding model like CLIP [19] guides the editing direction in the form of similarity score. Although this approach has demonstrated impressive editing capability in some visual domains like human faces [26], they are vulnerable to the blindspots of CLIP features. Specifically, CLIP exposes weakness in domain-specific applications that requires special knowledge [27,28], and its tendency to focus on the global semantic often renders it unsuitable for guiding local editing operation, especially when the image contains complex semantics [12].

Unfortunately, these vulnerabilities are greatly highlighted in our problem setting: fashion style editing of human imagery. In an attempt to introduce an intuitive interface for human fashion restyling, we explore the creative task of text-driven fashion style editing, where we steer the style of full-body human portrait with language guidance such as “street fashion” or “floral pattern” (Fig. 1). With our unique problem scope arises a new set of challenges, namely the modeling complexity of whole human body imagery and the elusiveness of fashion concepts, i.e., how some terms like ‘street fashion’ can induce different mental images to individuals. These two distinguish our approach from previous endeavors that tried to manipulate human faces with text guidance [17,13], in that we need to explicitly reformulate our guidance (i.e., fashion style) into a more illustrative and visually grounded learning signal.

To this end, we propose two directions to visually reinforce the guidance signal. First, we enrich the text prompt by querying a language model [29,30] to generate descriptions for the concept. Second, we retrieve reference images for the target text from a fashion database we constructed through web crawling, and guide our model to consult them for more descriptive guidance. Leveraging the enhanced visual clarity, our Fa shion S tyle E diting (FaSE) framework adeptly transforms abstract fashion concepts into tangible human imagery across a variety of applications.
